Laying in bed wondering if this flu was going to kill me and in a fit of apathy going to sleep.

I had flu once. The real flu, not what people say they have when they take 2 days off work, that's a cold. The flu fucks you up. I spent 2 weeks in bed feeling like death. Waking up shivering uncontrollably, feeling so cold that I sat in a hot shower in the middle of the night. Sometimes shivering while dripping with sweat. I was 22 and fit when I had it. It doesn't surprise me that the Spanish flu killed so many.

I agree that having the flu is a truly miserable experience for anyone unlucky enough to experience it. I also just wanted to mention that I recently learned a large number of deaths from the Spanish flu have been attributed to the over-use of the new wonder-drug at the time, aspirin. As it turns out, aspirin was given in much higher doses and more frequently than is considered safe today and for many people the result of the toxicity was fatal respiratory complications (pneumonia/ build-up of watery, bloody fluid in the lungs).

I quit a job that basically caused so much stress that I was barely functional as a person. I was sexually harassed, threatened, and felt unsafe. The cherry on top was the disrespect. I left for my mental health. Still a bit shaken up by the experience, and I relive the trauma every so often.

A kidney stone I had a few weeks ago. I had one 8 years ago that passed within hours. This one required 3 ER trips, 3 days in the hospital, and surgery to remove the stone and put a stent in. It was the vomiting that killed me. I couldn't eat for 5 days, which meant I couldn't take any pill medication. I was getting nausea medication they give cancer patients undergoing chemo, and that only helped a little. Everything had to be given by IV. I was puking so much and so hard that my neck and throat muscles basically prohibited me from opening my mouth more than maybe .5", which made vomiting even more fun. I truly wondered when it was going to end. It was a long week and half from the start of the pain to the pain ending from removing my stent and a second stone passing.

Pretty much right now.

27 years old. Been told my whole life that I'm very charismatic, intelligent, and that I would do well in life.

So far, it's been everything but that. Part of it was having a very stressful upbringing. Yes we didn't have all that much, but got by. It was more the constant stress of having two parents going at each other all the time (sometimes literally). Add in a crappy culture and insane religion, and you get a very messed up childhood.

So anyhow. I never got through university. Probably anxiety, depression, inattentive ADD, or a combination of all of them. Never been in a relationship, never had friends stick around, never experienced love.

So it's been lonely. Quit a really crappy job back in November and been unsuccessfully trying to find something since then. Beyond broke, living with parents, and don't have anything going for me.

So yeah. I've gone through it all. Even weighed the pros and cons of signing an organ donor card and literally being at the end of a rope. The scary part is where is actually makes more sense. The benefit of willing people to be able to carry on would be much greater than me spending my life just sliding along, being insignificant and unimportant at best.

Just living it day by day.

I injured myself on my first job straight out of highschool and got nothing but the shaft from my employer. I was too timid and stupid. I didn't have an attorney, my insurance refused to pay, and the hospital sent debt collectors to harass me. It's silly when I think about it now, but at the time I was horribly depressed. I was scared of doing nothing, scared of losing my job, and scared of even talking to the hospital. Eventually I just talked with one of the debt collectors and asked her to help me and tell me what to do and I was able to settle the debt for roughly 10% of the original bill.

I guess that was one of the lowest points in my life. Feeling like I was chewed up and spit out by the system, kinda a loss of innocence. I'd never really thought about the need for workman's comp lawyers before. I just thought that when I got hurt my employer would pay for it. I did all the right things, there were witnesses, my managers signed the forms. Nope. They figured I was a stupid kid who didn't know any better, that they could refuse to pay and I'd end up footing my own bill. And they were right =\

I've grown a lot since then, but sometimes I still feel that scared kid inside of me wondering what to do.
